topics.definition: The maximum weight approved for the start of the takeoff run (FAA Weight & Balance Handbook, GAMA definition). Everything on board counts: the empty aircraft, crew, payload and fuel.
topics.why_it_matters: MTOW caps how much payload and fuel can be carried together. On long flights, fuel takes a large share of MTOW, so payload must be reduced; MTOW also drives airport charges and runway requirements.
topics.example: The FAA Aircraft Characteristics Database lists the Airbus A320 (row 'Airbus A320', BADA model A320-231) at 171,961 lb, about 78,000 kg.

references.title: FAA Aircraft Weight and Balance Handbook (FAA-H-8083-1B), Glossary

topics.basis: definition quoted or paraphrased from the first reference; examples from the cited sources or this project's data

topics.definition: The maximum weight approved for the landing touchdown (FAA Weight & Balance Handbook). The FAA database calls it the Maximum Allowable Landing Weight (MALW).
topics.why_it_matters: Landing gear and structure are designed for a limited touchdown weight. On a short flight little fuel is burned, so the takeoff weight may be limited by MLW rather than MTOW.
topics.example: FAA Aircraft Characteristics Database: Airbus A320 MALW 145,505 lb, about 66,000 kg - 12,000 kg below its MTOW.

references.title: FAA Aircraft Weight and Balance Handbook (FAA-H-8083-1B), Glossary

topics.basis: definition quoted or paraphrased from the first reference; examples from the cited sources or this project's data

topics.definition: The weight of the aircraft ready for operation but without payload or usable fuel: the FAA Aircraft Characteristics Database describes OEW as including the crew and all fluids necessary for operation, such as engine oil, but excluding fuel and payload.
topics.why_it_matters: OEW is the starting point of every weight calculation. A heavier OEW (for example after a freighter conversion adds a cargo door, stronger floor and cargo loading system) leaves less room for payload under the same MZFW.
topics.example: OpenAP lists an OEW of 42,600 kg for the A320 (open model data, not an operator-specific certified weight).

references.title: FAA Aircraft Weight and Balance Handbook (FAA-H-8083-1B), Glossary

topics.basis: definition quoted or paraphrased from the first reference; examples from the cited sources or this project's data

topics.definition: The maximum authorized weight of an aircraft without fuel (FAA Weight & Balance Handbook). It is the aircraft (OEW) plus payload, before any usable fuel is added.
topics.why_it_matters: Fuel stored in the wings relieves bending at the wing root; payload in the fuselage does not. MZFW therefore limits how much payload can be loaded, regardless of how much fuel is carried.
topics.example: EFW publishes an MZFW of 73.8 t for the A321P2F (weight variant 011); Airbus publishes 178 t for the A330-200F.

references.title: FAA Aircraft Weight and Balance Handbook (FAA-H-8083-1B), Glossary

topics.basis: definition quoted or paraphrased from the first reference; examples from the cited sources or this project's data

topics.definition: The weight of occupants, cargo and baggage (FAA Weight & Balance Handbook, GAMA definition). Manufacturers often publish a maximum structural payload - the most payload the structure allows - which is not the same as the revenue cargo actually carried on a flight.
topics.why_it_matters: Payload is what generates revenue. The structural maximum is a limit; the revenue payload on a real flight depends on demand, cargo density (volume may fill before weight) and the fuel needed for the distance.
topics.example: Boeing lists the 777 Freighter with a gross structural payload of 107 tonnes. A particular 777F flight may carry far less revenue cargo; this project never treats a structural maximum (or its own modelled payload) as revenue cargo.

references.title: FAA Aircraft Weight and Balance Handbook (FAA-H-8083-1B), Glossary

topics.basis: definition quoted or paraphrased from the first reference; examples from the cited sources or this project's data

topics.definition: The distance an aircraft can fly from takeoff to landing with a given payload, fuel load and reserve policy. A single 'range' figure is only meaningful together with its payload and reserve conditions.
topics.why_it_matters: Range decides which routes an aircraft can serve without a stop. More payload means less fuel can be loaded under MTOW, so range falls.
topics.example: Boeing: 'The 777F has 5,000 nmi of range with a 107-tonne payload'. OpenAP's 'nominal cruise range' in this database has no stated payload condition, so it is labelled as model data, not a payload-range point.
topics.basis: general explanation; examples sourced as cited

topics.definition: The trade-off between how much payload an aircraft carries and how far it can fly. With maximum payload the aircraft can take off with fuel only up to MTOW; flying further requires swapping payload for fuel until the fuel tanks are full; beyond that only less payload (lower weight) extends range.
topics.why_it_matters: It explains why the same freighter can carry its full payload on medium routes but must leave cargo behind on very long routes - central to choosing an aircraft for a cargo network.
topics.example: Published single points: 777F 5,000 nmi with 107 t; 767-300F 3,300 nmi with 57 t (Boeing). A complete payload-range diagram needs manufacturer performance data that this project does not hold.

references.title: FAA Aircraft Weight and Balance Handbook (FAA-H-8083-1B), Glossary

topics.basis: general explanation; examples sourced as cited

topics.definition: The mass of fuel consumed. This project splits a flight's block fuel into taxi-out, trip fuel (brake release to touchdown), landing roll and taxi-in.
topics.why_it_matters: Fuel is typically the largest variable cost of a flight and determines emissions. Fuel burned also lowers the aircraft's weight during the flight.
topics.example: Part 2 model estimate (OpenAP, no wind, ISA): A320 Frankfurt-Paris CDG with 10 t payload burns about 2,271 kg block fuel, of which about 1,925 kg is trip fuel and 334 kg taxi fuel.
topics.basis: definition quoted or paraphrased from the first reference; examples from the cited sources or this project's data

topics.definition: Thrust specific fuel consumption (TSFC) is the fuel flow rate divided by the thrust produced - how much fuel an engine needs per unit of thrust per unit of time (NASA Glenn).
topics.why_it_matters: Lower SFC means the same thrust for less fuel. Higher bypass ratios generally reduce SFC, which is why modern turbofans have large fans.
topics.example: If two engines produce the same cruise thrust and one has a 10 % lower TSFC, it burns about 10 % less fuel per hour at that condition.
topics.basis: definition quoted or paraphrased from the first reference; examples from the cited sources or this project's data

topics.definition: Thrust is the force that moves the aircraft forward; a jet engine produces it by accelerating air rearwards (NASA Glenn). A turbofan uses a core (compressor, combustor, turbine) to drive a large fan; most of the air bypasses the core and produces most of the thrust efficiently.
topics.why_it_matters: Rated thrust limits takeoff performance (runway length, climb) and is certified per engine; the bypass ratio indicates how much air goes around the core.
topics.example: The A320's default OpenAP engine, CFM56-5B4, has a rated thrust of 117.9 kN per engine and a bypass ratio of 5.9 (ICAO Engine Emissions Databank values as distributed by OpenAP).
topics.basis: definition quoted or paraphrased from the first reference; examples from the cited sources or this project's data

topics.definition: Block time runs from off-block (doors closed, aircraft starts moving at the gate) to on-block (aircraft stops at the destination gate). It includes taxi, takeoff, flight and landing. BTS reports it as ramp-to-ramp hours.
topics.why_it_matters: Many costs are measured per block hour (crew pay, maintenance rates, utilization), so block hours link flights to annual cost assumptions.
topics.example: Part 2 model: A320 Frankfurt-Paris CDG = 71.9 block minutes (1.20 block hours), of which 44.2 minutes airborne.

references.title: Economic Values for FAA Investment and Regulatory Decisions, Section 4 (Tables 4-16, 4-17)

topics.basis: definition quoted or paraphrased from the first reference; examples from the cited sources or this project's data

topics.definition: One flight cycle is one takeoff and landing (one pressurisation cycle of the fuselage).
topics.why_it_matters: Fatigue of the airframe and life-limited engine parts is counted in cycles, so short-haul aircraft that fly many sectors per day age differently from long-haul aircraft with the same hours.
topics.example: A single saved flight estimate in this project is one completed leg = one flight cycle; per-cycle maintenance reserves are charged once per leg.

references.title: Project documentation: full operating cost model (taxonomy)

topics.basis: general explanation; examples sourced as cited

topics.definition: A narrowbody (single-aisle) aircraft has one passenger aisle; a widebody (twin-aisle) aircraft has a fuselage wide enough for two aisles. The FAA classifies aircraft types this way in its Economic Values Table 4-16.
topics.why_it_matters: Body width determines cabin layout, the size of containers and pallets that fit side by side on the main deck, and typical routes (short/medium vs long haul).
topics.example: FAA Table 4-16: A320 and 737-800 are narrowbody; A330-200, 767-300, 777-F and 747-4F are widebody.

references.title: Economic Values for FAA Investment and Regulatory Decisions, Section 4 (Tables 4-16, 4-17)

topics.basis: definition quoted or paraphrased from the first reference; examples from the cited sources or this project's data

topics.definition: A freighter carries cargo on the main deck instead of passengers. Production (purpose-built) freighters are built as freighters at the factory; converted freighters (P2F) are former passenger aircraft modified later.
topics.why_it_matters: Production freighters are designed around cargo from the start; converted freighters reuse airframes with remaining life at lower acquisition cost. Their weights and performance differ and passenger specifications must not be used as freighter specifications.
topics.example: Production: 777 Freighter, 767-300 Freighter (Boeing), A330-200F (Airbus). Converted: A321P2F (EFW), 767-300 Boeing Converted Freighter.
topics.basis: general explanation; examples sourced as cited

topics.definition: A ULD is a container or a pallet with a net used to load cargo or baggage on an aircraft so that many pieces can be handled as one unit; IATA publishes the ULD regulations and identification codes (for example AAY, AKH, LD3).
topics.why_it_matters: ULDs make loading fast and safe, protect the aircraft structure and define how many positions fit on each deck. Container shapes are designed for specific deck contours.
topics.example: EFW: the A321P2F has 14 AAY container positions on the main deck and 10 AKH positions in the lower deck. Airbus: the A330-200F lower deck takes 26 LD3 containers (or 8 pallets + 2 LD3).
topics.basis: definition quoted or paraphrased from the first reference; examples from the cited sources or this project's data

topics.definition: A flat aluminium platform onto which cargo is built up and secured with a net; pallets are ULDs. Common base sizes are given in inches, e.g. 96 x 125 in, and long pallets such as 16 ft and 20 ft exist for oversized cargo.
topics.why_it_matters: Pallets allow irregular and oversized cargo that does not fit containers; door size and floor strength decide which pallets an aircraft can take.
topics.example: Airbus advertises 96 x 125 in pallets side by side on the A330-200F main deck; EFW states the A330P2F can take 16 ft and 20 ft pallets.
topics.basis: definition quoted or paraphrased from the first reference; examples from the cited sources or this project's data

topics.definition: A large door cut into the side of the fuselage so that ULDs can be loaded onto the main (upper) deck. Production freighters are built with one; a passenger-to-freighter conversion adds it.
topics.why_it_matters: The door size limits the largest ULD or pallet that can be loaded. Installing it requires major structural reinforcement around the cut-out.
topics.example: EFW: the A321P2F's hydraulically operated main-deck cargo door is 142 in wide and 85 in high; the A330P2F door is 141 in by 101 in.
topics.basis: definition quoted or paraphrased from the first reference; examples from the cited sources or this project's data

topics.definition: The floor equipment that moves and locks ULDs on the deck: roller tracks, ball mats near the door, guides and locks; powered systems drive containers into position.
topics.why_it_matters: A good CLS shortens turnaround time and allows flexible container/pallet layouts; it is part of a freighter conversion.
topics.example: EFW describes a powered cargo loading system for the A330P2F in which containers are 'power-driven into position', and a cargo loading system for containers or pallets on both decks of the A321P2F.
topics.basis: general explanation; examples sourced as cited

topics.definition: Modifying a used passenger aircraft into a freighter. EFW summarises the work as: the floor is rebuilt, stringers and frames are replaced or reinforced, the main cargo door is installed, the fuselage is reinforced, and windows and rear passenger doors are locked (plugged). A rigid cargo barrier protects the crew and the main deck becomes a certified cargo compartment.
topics.why_it_matters: Conversion gives aircraft a second life and supplies freighters at lower cost than new production freighters. The design change is approved as a Supplemental Type Certificate (STC).
topics.example: EFW's A321P2F STC covers all weight variants of the A321-200; its rigid cargo barrier is designed for loads up to 9 g, and the main deck is a Class E cargo hold.
topics.basis: definition quoted or paraphrased from the first reference; examples from the cited sources or this project's data

topics.definition: Costs directly caused by operating the aircraft. In this project's taxonomy: direct variable costs (fuel, maintenance, LLP, navigation, landing, handling, crew allowances) plus direct fixed costs (crew salaries, insurance, operating lease).
topics.why_it_matters: DOC is the basis for comparing aircraft on the same route; definitions differ between organisations, so always check what is included.
topics.example: Saved example (illustrative scenario): A320 FRA-CDG direct variable subtotal 2,768.21 EUR and direct fixed subtotal 678.66 EUR - both PARTIAL because navigation, landing and handling are unavailable.

references.title: Project documentation: full operating cost model (taxonomy)

topics.basis: project definition (this project's cost taxonomy); examples from the saved illustrative scenario

topics.definition: In this project: COC = direct variable + direct fixed + indirect costs (administration, cargo sales, G&A). It excludes noncash depreciation and financing interest.
topics.why_it_matters: COC shows the cash needed to fly; Total operating cost (TOC) adds depreciation and Total costs add financing.
topics.example: Saved example: partial COC subtotal 3,946.08 EUR; complete COC unavailable because four components are missing.

references.title: Project documentation: full operating cost model (taxonomy)

topics.basis: project definition (this project's cost taxonomy); examples from the saved illustrative scenario

topics.definition: The spreading of an asset's cost over its useful life. This project uses straight-line depreciation: (depreciable value - residual value) / useful life, allocated per flight; it is a noncash cost added in TOC.
topics.why_it_matters: Ownership cost is often the largest fixed cost of an aircraft; owned and leased aircraft show it in different cost lines.
topics.example: Illustrative owned scenario: (50 M - 5 M EUR) / 20 years = 2.25 M EUR per year, about 898 EUR on the 1.2-block-hour A320 example.
topics.basis: project definition (this project's cost taxonomy); examples from the saved illustrative scenario
